sentence: A bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae that can affect the genitals, rectum, throat and eyes.
note: Green Book: bacterium infects urethra, cervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva; NHS: throat, eyes, anus.

sentence: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by a bacterium called Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
It can affect the genitals, rectum, throat and eyes.
Not everyone has symptoms, so testing matters when infection is possible.
note: NHS: not everyone gets symptoms; important to get tested if you think you might have it

sentence: In England, diagnosis rates are highest among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men and among people aged 20 to 34.
note: GRASP: rates highest among GBMSM and people aged 20 to 34

sentence: Treatment is with antibiotics, and if it is given early, lasting problems are unlikely.
note: NHS: usually treated with antibiotics; treated early unlikely to cause lasting problems

sentence: Infection with the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Passed on through vaginal, anal or oral sex without a condom, or contact with infected secretions
note: Green Book: condomless vaginal, oral or anal sex or contact with infected secretions

sentence: Sharing sex toys that have not been washed or covered with a new condom each time
note: Retrieved summary of NHS-service pages; summary blended, page not individually confirmed

sentence: Passed from a mother to her baby during birth
note: NHS: mother to baby during birth

sentence: People without symptoms can still pass it on
Sex without a condom or other barrier
note: NHS: passed on through unprotected sex

sentence: Previous infection, which gives no lasting protection against catching it again
note: Green Book: infection does not produce lasting protection; NHS: reinfection possible

sentence: In England, being a gay, bisexual or other man who has sex with men, or a young adult, as these groups have the highest diagnosis rates
note: GRASP and BASHH guideline summary; population pattern, not a judgement

sentence: Discharge from the penis, or a change in vaginal discharge
Sore testicles in men
Lower abdominal pain in women
Red, itchy or painful eyes when the eyes are infected
note: NHS urgent advice lists red, itchy or painful eyes

sentence: Pelvic inflammatory disease in women, which can lead to long-term pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy and infertility
Painful infection of the testicles and prostate gland in men, which may reduce fertility in a small number of cases
Rarely, spread through the bloodstream, which can cause sepsis
note: NHS complications; BASHH leaflet: rarely to blood, skin or joints

sentence: Premature birth in pregnancy, and eye damage in a baby infected during birth
Gonorrhoea can be diagnosed by testing a sample taken on a swab from the discharge or the affected area.
In men, a urine sample can also be used.
A person can be tested even without symptoms.
Testing is available at sexual health clinics and some GP surgeries, pharmacies and contraceptive services.
A clinic may also suggest a throat swab and tests for other STIs.
note: BASHH leaflet summary: throat swab and testing for other STIs

sentence: Gonorrhoea is treated with antibiotics.
In most cases this is a single antibiotic injection, given in the buttock or thigh.
note: NHS treatment: injection usually in buttocks or thigh; BASHH leaflet: single injection in buttock

sentence: Sometimes a tablet can be used instead of an injection.
Treatment can start before the test results arrive when infection is likely.
A follow-up appointment a week or two after treatment is usually recommended so another test can be done.
Current sexual partners also need testing, and the clinic can contact partners anonymously if the person wishes.
The NHS recommends condoms for vaginal and anal sex, and a condom or dental dam for oral sex.
Testing once a year, and when there is a new sexual partner, is also recommended.
In England, the 4CMenB vaccine is offered to some people at higher risk of gonorrhoea, mainly gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men.
note: GRASP: programme began August 2025, aimed mainly at GBMSM at increased risk; NHS: MenB vaccine offered to higher-risk GBMSM

sentence: A routine GP appointment or a sexual health clinic visit is the usual route for testing when infection is suspected.
note: NHS: get tested at a GP surgery or sexual health clinic

sentence: For someone who has gonorrhoea, or thinks they might, red, itchy or painful eyes, a high temperature, joint pain or swelling, or a spotty or blotchy rash need an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.
People who are pregnant and think they may have gonorrhoea are advised to be tested early, because untreated infection can affect the pregnancy and the baby.
note: NHS complications: early testing and treatment matters in pregnancy

sentence: Not everyone with gonorrhoea has symptoms, which is why testing matters if infection is possible.
When symptoms appear, they usually start around two weeks after infection, although they sometimes do not appear until many months later.
Women may notice a change in vaginal discharge, a burning feeling when peeing, or pain in the lower abdomen.
note: NHS summary: discharge, burning when peeing, lower abdominal pain

sentence: Men more often notice discharge from the penis or sore testicles.
Infection of the throat, eyes or rectum can also occur.
Because symptoms can be mild or absent, a person can pass the infection on without knowing.
note: Green Book: people without symptoms can still pass it on

sentence: Signs that may suggest the infection is causing wider problems include red, itchy or painful eyes, a high temperature, joint pain or swelling, or a spotty or blotchy rash.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111 for these signs in someone who has, or may have, gonorrhoea.
Symptoms usually improve within a few days of treatment, although pelvic or testicular pain can take up to two weeks to settle fully.
note: Retrieved summary of NHS pages; blended, page not individually confirmed

sentence: Gonorrhoea is caused by a bacterium called Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
It is passed on through vaginal, anal or oral sex without a condom, or through contact with infected secretions.
Sharing sex toys that have not been washed or covered with a new condom each time can also pass it on.
A mother can pass the infection to her baby during birth.
The bacteria survive only briefly outside the body.
It is not spread through hugging, kissing, toilet seats or shared cutlery.
note: Retrieved summary of NHS-service pages; blended, page not individually confirmed

sentence: Having had gonorrhoea before does not give lasting protection, so it can be caught again.
UKHSA reports that around half of gonorrhoea diagnoses in England are in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men.
note: Green Book: nearly half in 2022; FAQ: around half annually

sentence: BASHH says the infection also disproportionately affects young people aged 15 to 24.
UKHSA reported fewer diagnoses in England in 2024 than in 2023.
Testing is available at sexual health clinics, and some GP surgeries, pharmacies and contraceptive services also offer it.
Home test kits can also be ordered online.
The test usually uses a swab of discharge or of the affected area, and men can also give a urine sample.
A person can be tested even when they have no symptoms.
A clinic may also suggest a throat swab and tests for other STIs.
Treatment can start before the results arrive when infection is likely.
Current sexual partners need testing too, and the clinic can contact them anonymously for the person if they wish.
Some previous partners may also need testing, and the clinic advises on this.
Treatment from sexual health clinics is free and is given in the clinic.
note: BASHH leaflet: all treatments from sexual health clinics are free

sentence: Gonorrhoea is treated with antibiotics.
In most cases this is a single antibiotic injection, given in the buttock or thigh.
Sometimes a tablet can be used instead of an injection, if the person prefers.
Symptoms usually improve within a few days.
A follow-up appointment a week or two after treatment is usually recommended so another test can be done.

BASHH's 2025 guideline says a routine test of cure is not necessary for infections of the genitals or anus treated with ceftriaxone when the infection is susceptible to it, so follow-up advice can differ.
note: Retrieved guideline excerpt: routine test of cure not necessary for anogenital infection treated with ceftriaxone if susceptible

sentence: The BASHH leaflet advises that sex is avoided until seven days after both the person and their partners have taken their treatment.
Reinfection is possible, which is one reason partners are tested and treated too.
Some strains of gonorrhoea are becoming resistant to antibiotics.
UKHSA reports that most ceftriaxone-resistant cases are linked to travel to or from the Asia-Pacific region, with some evidence of spread within England.
If gonorrhoea is treated early, it is unlikely to cause lasting problems.
Left untreated, it can spread and cause serious harm.
In women it can spread to the womb and fallopian tubes and cause pelvic inflammatory disease.
This can lead to long-term pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy and infertility.
In men it can cause a painful infection of the testicles and prostate gland, which may reduce fertility in a small number of cases.
In rare cases the infection spreads through the bloodstream, where it can cause sepsis, or to the skin or joints.
US CDC guidance describes skin lesions and joint pain or swelling when the infection spreads through the body.
note: CDC (US) treatment guidelines summary on disseminated gonococcal infection

sentence: In pregnancy, untreated infection raises the risk of premature birth, and a baby infected during birth can have eye damage.
For this reason the NHS says early testing and treatment matter in pregnancy.
The NHS recommends condoms for vaginal and anal sex, and a condom or dental dam for oral sex.
Testing once a year, and when there is a new sexual partner, is also recommended.
There is currently no licensed vaccine against the gonorrhoea bacterium itself.
In England, the 4CMenB vaccine, which is made for meningococcal group B disease, began to be offered for gonorrhoea prevention in August 2025.
It is aimed mainly at gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men who are at higher risk of gonorrhoea.
Protection against gonorrhoea is not a licensed use of the vaccine, so this use is off-label.
UKHSA estimates that the vaccine gives partial protection.
note: UKHSA STI data release gives a protection estimate of 30-40%, which is partial
